title: Check yourself: which calls order memory

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A metrics thread loops `while (paused) { if (verbose) System.out.println("paused"); }` on a plain boolean field `paused`, which an admin thread sets to false. In production, with verbose off, the thread never resumes. In staging, with verbose on, it resumes every time. What does staging show?

options.text: The println fixes the bug, since the lock it takes publishes the admin thread's write to the reader
options.says: the admin thread never takes PrintStream's lock, so the lock gives no edge from its write

options.text: The println only hides the bug, since the lock it takes is one the admin thread never takes
options.says: the lock acquire keeps HotSpot reading the field again, but with no edge from the writer the JLS still allows the loop to spin

options.text: The println only hides the bug, since the console output slows the loop until the write reaches main memory
options.says: the hang comes from the JIT hoisting the read out of the loop; a slower loop gets no edge from the admin thread's write, and the lock acquire is what makes HotSpot read the field again

options.text: The println fixes the bug, since the console output slows the loop until the write reaches main memory
options.says: the hang comes from the JIT hoisting the read out of the loop; a slower loop gets no edge from the admin thread's write, and the lock acquire is what makes HotSpot read the field again

origin.section: Sleep, Yield and println Create No Edge, Even When the Loop Ends

questions.stem: An order service sets `status` inside `synchronized (orderLock)`. A report thread reads `status` inside `synchronized (reportLock)`. Both fields are plain and both locks are private final objects. Is the report thread's read ordered after the write?

options.text: No, since a monitor exit is ordered before later entries of that same monitor
options.says: the writer releases orderLock and the reader acquires reportLock, so no unlock-lock pair connects them

options.text: No, since a monitor exit is ordered before later entries of monitors in that same class
options.says: the edge runs between an unlock and later locks of one monitor object; which class declares the lock fields plays no part

options.text: Yes, since a monitor exit is ordered before later entries of other monitors too
options.says: an unlock is ordered only before later locks of that same monitor

options.text: Yes, since a monitor exit is ordered before later entries of any monitor guarding the field
options.says: an unlock is ordered before later locks of that monitor, not of any monitor; these two threads lock different monitors

origin.section: Only an Acquire That Succeeds, on the Same Object, Gets the Edge

questions.stem: A coordinator starts three workers. Each writes its subtotal into its own slot of a plain long[] and then calls `done.countDown()` on a CountDownLatch(3). The coordinator calls `done.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` and then adds up the array. Today one worker needs 5 seconds. What can the coordinator count on?

options.text: Every subtotal, since an await() that times out still waits for the countDown() calls in progress
options.says: a timed await returns false when the time runs out, without waiting for anything further

options.text: Every subtotal, since an await() that times out gets the edge from every countDown(), early or late
options.says: the slow worker had not counted down, and a timed-out await gets no edge at all

options.text: No subtotal for certain, since an await() of any kind gets no edge for writes to a plain long[]
options.says: a successful await() is ordered after every write made before the countDown() calls, plain array slots included; this one failed because it timed out

options.text: No subtotal for certain, since an await() that times out gets no edge from any countDown() call
options.says: the javadoc grants the edge to actions following a successful return from await(); a return of false gets nothing

origin.section: Only an Acquire That Succeeds, on the Same Object, Gets the Edge

questions.stem: A login handler creates a Session with plain fields, puts it into a ConcurrentHashMap under its token, and then sets `session.user = loadUser(token)`. A request thread gets the session for that token (non-null) and reads `session.user`. What does it see?

options.text: The user, since the map orders the setter that follows the put before a get that returns the session
options.says: the map orders only what was written before the put; the setter ran after it

options.text: No particular value, since the map orders what preceded the put before a get that returns it
options.says: the user is written after the put, so no edge reaches the request thread's read: it may see the user or null

options.text: The user, since a get that runs once the handler is done is ordered after the put and the setter
options.says: being later in time gives no edge; only the put is ordered before the get

options.text: No particular value, since a put is ordered before a get only when both run on one thread
options.says: a get on any thread that returns the session is ordered after the put, so everything written before the put is visible

origin.section: The Edge Covers Writes Made Before the Release, Not After It

questions.stem: An integration test starts a worker that adds 10 records to a plain ArrayList, calls Thread.sleep(500) on the test thread, and asserts that the list holds 10 records. It has passed 2,000 times in a row. What does the assertion see, by the Java memory model?

options.text: Nothing about the records, since waking from sleep() orders no other thread's writes
options.says: JLS 17.3: sleep has no synchronization semantics, and finishing earlier in time creates no edge either

options.text: It sees all 10 records, since the worker is done long before sleep(500) is up
options.says: finishing earlier in time creates no edge to the test's read

options.text: It sees all 10 records, since a thread waking from sleep() reads shared fields again
options.says: JLS 17.3: sleep has no synchronization semantics; the compiler need not reload values after it

options.text: Nothing about the records, since sleep() orders the read before the worker's adds
options.says: sleep has no synchronization semantics (JLS 17.3), so it orders the read neither before nor after the adds

origin.section: Sleep, Yield and println Create No Edge, Even When the Loop Ends

concepts: A value changed in place after it was put in a ConcurrentHashMap may be seen changed, partly changed or unchanged by a thread that gets it.
A println in a spin loop takes a lock the writer never takes, so it can make a visibility bug disappear on HotSpot without creating an edge.
An unlock is ordered only before later locks of the same monitor; a lock the writer never takes gives the reader no edge, and HotSpot may remove a lock on an unshared object altogether.
Thread.sleep and Thread.yield have no synchronization semantics, and a delay orders neither memory nor time; wait on a Future or a latch instead.
